title: Do all repeated experiences have to be the same? Yes and no.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton asks whether the repeated experiences that make learning stick must be identical, using golfers, a Duolingo vocabulary drill and a friend's book club as examples. His answer is yes and no: everyone, not just elite athletes, needs consistent rather than occasional repetition across knowledge, skills and understanding. The repetition has to target the same underlying learning, but it does not have to look the same each time. He illustrates this with letter-shape practice for young children and with perspective-taking questions in history and politics that draw on one core skill. The warning is that dull, literally identical repetition risks making only boredom sticky. He closes by flagging that this principle should shape how curriculums are written and lessons planned.
points: Skelton holds that consistent repetition is non-negotiable for knowledge, skills and deepening understanding alike, not just for sport or music.
The key move is to separate the learning being repeated from the context in which it is practised, so the same skill can be rehearsed through varied tasks.
His early-writing example shows copy sheets can stay as an occasional tool while sand trays, tracing and pattern-making carry the same hand movements.
Perspective-taking questions about football, Henry VIII and elections show how one core skill can be repeated across surface-different content.
Identical repetition risks making only a dull routine sticky, which is why curriculum and lesson design need to build in variety of context.
quotes: It’s true. We don’t get better by doing things occasionally. We get better by doing things consistently.

The answer to the first question is yes, we do all have to do that. There is no substitute for repeated experiences. Even super-talented people who are able to move from Beginning to Developing or from nothing to sticky very quickly reach a point where repeated experiences become essential if they are to make their infinitely more complex learning sticky.

I’m pretty happy that, thanks to the repeated consistent experiences, eight out of the ten words have become pretty sticky already. Consistent, not occasional, repeated experiences are essential for knowledge learning.

In the same way, consistent repetition, over a different time scale, works well for understanding, too. Occasional reflection might lead to something but repeated reflection is more likely to be helpful.

Third, repeated experiences do have to be the same, literally repeated time after time, but they don’t have to be identical in presentation. In fact, it’s a good thing when they aren’t always presented in exactly the same way.
Each of these questions seems different on the surface. But each of them requires the same skill - to be able to identify different viewpoints - if the questions are going to be answered effectively.

To make repeated experiences enjoyable for learners, we need to keep the actual learning we want to happen at the forefront of our minds. Then, it helps if we can find different contexts that will enable that learning to be repeated consistently. If we don’t do that we run the risk of enabling our students to make sticky only that learning is nothing more than a dull repetition of exactly the same thing. To put it mildly, this is not a good idea.
